What should an AI agent actually be allowed to decide?
This is one of the first questions I'd ask before deploying an agent inside a business.
Giving an agent access to your tools is easy.

Deciding what it can do without asking you is harder.
I use a simple framework:

LOW RISK → Let the agent decide
If the cost of being wrong is small, give it autonomy.
Examples:
→ Categorising support tickets
→ Updating CRM fields
→ Sending routine reminders
→ Summarising meetings
→ Moving tasks between stages
→ Finding and organising information
The agent can act.
No approval needed.

MEDIUM RISK → Agent recommends, human approves
The decision has consequences, but it's still reviewable.
Examples:
→ Choosing which leads deserve immediate attention
→ Drafting a customer response
→ Recommending a discount
→ Prioritising sales opportunities
→ Creating a project plan
→ Flagging an unusual customer issue
The agent does the analysis.
A human makes the final call.

HIGH RISK → Human decides
If the decision can materially affect money, reputation, customers or the business, keep a human in the loop.
Examples:
→ Approving large refunds
→ Signing contracts
→ Hiring or firing
→ Changing pricing strategy
→ Making financial commitments
→ Deleting critical data
→ Sending sensitive information
The agent can prepare the work.
It shouldn't own the decision.

That's the mistake I see businesses making with AI agents.
They ask:
"Can the agent do this?"
The better question is:
"What happens if the agent gets this wrong?"

That answer should determine how much autonomy you give it.
Build the agent around the risk.
Not around what the technology happens to be capable of.

Vibe coding: the freedom recruiters wanted, and the risk nobody planned for

A recruiter can now build a candidate screening tool in an afternoon.
No IT ticket. No vendor contract. No six-month wait.
Just a problem, a prompt and a working prototype.

That's a real shift. For years, recruiters depended on IT teams, software vendors and developers to turn workflow problems into technology solutions. Now they can:
1️⃣ Experiment faster
2️⃣ Own their workflows
3️⃣ Prototype ideas that never would have justified a big technology project
But there's another side.

What happens when that tool touches candidate data?
Salary details. Interview notes. Assessment results. Personal information.
Picture a recruiter pasting CVs and salary expectations into a free AI tool to save time.
Or a home-built screening tool that quietly filters out certain candidates, and nobody notices.

This is no longer just an IT problem. In many regions, hiring data and AI-assisted decisions fall under regulations like GDPR and Singapore's PDPA. Shadow AI in recruitment is a compliance risk, not just a technical one.
So should recruiters stop experimenting?
No. I think the answer is guardrails, not bans.

Here's what I'd put in place:
1️⃣ Use dummy data for prototypes, never real candidate data
2️⃣ No AI tool makes or ranks hiring decisions without human review
3️⃣ Keep a simple register of internal tools, so nothing is invisible
4️⃣ Set a clear trigger for when a prototype goes to security or legal review
5️⃣ Test the output before trusting it, especially for bias
6️⃣ Move successful prototypes into proper governance before scaling

AI gives recruiters more technological freedom.
With that freedom comes responsibility.

The future may not belong to the organisations that experiment the most, but to those that know how to experiment safely.

Most portfolio ML projects only show you the model that worked. Here's one that also shows you what didn't.

While building WellPulse, a project that predicts a student wellbeing score (1–10) from social-media and behavioral survey data. I found that one feature in the dataset explained 89% of the target's variance completely on its own. A near-tautological shortcut, not a real signal. I excluded it and documented why, instead of quietly using it to inflate my metrics.

Later, hyperparameter tuning genuinely failed to beat the untuned baseline model. I reported that too, instead of re-running it until it "worked."

That's the standard I held the entire build to, end to end, across 13 phases:

→ Data validation via a schema contract that fails loudly on bad data instead of silently
→ EDA and the leakage check above, run before any model ever saw the data
→ 9 model families compared, including LightGBM and XGBoost, against an untuned baseline
→ SHAP explainability, MLflow experiment tracking, and a model registry
→ A FastAPI backend with real per-user auth, Postgres persistence, and check-in history
→ Multi-stage Docker build and GitHub Actions CI/CD
→ Live deployment
→ A weekly automated job that watches live production data for drift

71 tests passing end to end. And the README states the model's real limitations plainly including where its recall is weakest because a project like this is only useful to a hiring manager if it's honest about what a model actually does and doesn't do.

& the strong people are not on job boards. They are mid contract, running workshops or building internally.

To hiring managers: you cannot see any of this on a CV. Ask every candidate what broke in production & how they fixed it. Specific answer with a timeline, good sign. Pivot back to the POC, not ready.

To candidates: the market rewards honesty right now because everyone else is inflating. Know your level & say it.

At pre-seed, a strong read deck, product demo or technical white paper, and a few substantive customer conversations may be enough for initial diligence. I've seen founders raise with little more than this. Don't spend two weeks preparing documents nobody has asked to see.

𝟮. 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗺𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹.
Your diligence materials should address the risks specific to YOUR company.
Technical moat? Architecture, proprietary data, validation results, and benchmarks against relevant competitors. For AI companies: accuracy, latency, reliability, and inference costs.

Compliance-heavy? Regulatory pathway, security architecture, data governance, and what it will actually take for customers to adopt your product.

GTM-driven? ICP, economic buyer, paid pilots, conversion rates, contract sizes, and sales cycle. A pipeline full of unpaid pilots is not ARR.

Show investors the evidence that matters to YOUR company and THEIR investment thesis.

𝟯. 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸.
What will this round of capital allow you to prove in 12 to 18 months?

For software startups, that may mean revenue, retention, and repeatable customer acquisition. For biotech and deep tech, technical validation, regulatory progress, or manufacturing readiness.

Your financial model, burn, runway, hiring plan, and use of funds should explicitly reflect those milestones. Know exactly what evidence you'll need to raise again.

𝟰. 𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗽 𝘀𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗿𝗲 𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗗𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗲.
Have your cap table, incorporation documents, financing history, IP assignments, and contracts organized internally.

Start with your deck. Share relevant documents as diligence progresses. Restrict access to sensitive technical, financial, customer, and legal information.

If an investor requests extensive diligence at pre-seed, ask what specific questions they need answered to make an investment decision.

You should be able to explain your business without sending someone 30 attachments.

Every document you share creates another opportunity for an investor to scrutinize your assumptions. Make sure it adds something to the conversation.

Keep your materials concise, current, and internally consistent. A clear two-page technical overview beats a 30-page AI-generated document that says very little.

South Korea:

The gap: Taiwan's boom is volume-driven, so it needs workers. Korea's is price-driven, so it mostly rewards shareholders. Korea's $500bn investment plan could close the gap once spending actually lands.

1️⃣ Price spikes end. Memory chips are notoriously cyclical, so avoid locking multi-year AI infrastructure contracts at peak prices.

2️⃣ Judge partners by capacity, not hype. Volume creates jobs and lasting value. Price inflation creates one-off profits.

3️⃣ Expect a lag. Korea's payoff waits on capex that hasn't happened yet. Plan AI ROI in years, not quarters.

Moneyball Was a Precursor to AI Analytics Strategy

For decades, many important business decisions—who to hire, which projects to fund, and where to invest—have been driven by human intuition and the “executive eye test.”

We trust leaders who sound confident, have impressive credentials, and rely on experience. But intuition can also carry hidden biases, inconsistency, and blind spots.

That is why artificial intelligence and data-driven decision-making matter: they shift decisions from subjective impressions toward measurable evidence and probability.

A useful example is the story behind Moneyball. In the early 2000s, the budget-constrained Oakland A’s challenged traditional scouting. Instead of relying primarily on subjective qualities such as appearance and athleticism, they used statistical data to identify what actually contributed to winning—especially the unglamorous metric of getting on base.

The lesson extends far beyond baseball.

1. Reducing Human Bias

Human judgment is affected by recency bias, fatigue, and overconfidence. When reviewing hundreds of customer tickets, compliance files, or financial risks, consistency inevitably varies.

AI models and predictive analytics do not eliminate human judgment; they give it a stronger foundation. By analyzing large volumes of data, these systems can reveal patterns, anomalies, and probabilities that people may miss.

2. Measuring Outcomes Instead of Signals

Traditional organizations often reward visible, subjective qualities: the most charismatic presenter or the most polished proposal.

A data-driven approach asks better questions:

What correlates with customer retention?

Which contract clauses signal liability risk?

Which bottlenecks increase operating costs?

Which hiring indicators predict performance?

AI analytics helps organizations focus on measurable outcomes rather than assumptions or consensus.

3. Turning Decisions into Testable Hypotheses

When a decision is based primarily on instinct, failure is often explained through anecdotes: “the market shifted” or “execution fell short.”

With statistical models, decisions become measurable hypotheses. Organizations can track accuracy, test alternatives, identify data drift, and improve their approach over time.

The Bottom Line

Using AI and statistical data is not about removing human accountability or blindly deferring to algorithms.

It is about recognizing that intuition becomes less reliable as scale and complexity increase.

The real lesson of Moneyball was not simply to trust numbers. It was to question how success is measured—and use better evidence to make better decisions.

That is the foundation of an effective AI analytics strategy.

That distinction is becoming fundamental to AI Governance.

A CV is personal data.

But using it to summarise a candidate’s experience is not the same risk as using it to automatically rank candidates.

A customer’s voice recording used for transcription is not the same as using biometric characteristics to identify or categorise that person.

A confidential contract entered into an enterprise AI environment is not the same as uploading it into an external consumer GenAI tool.

𝐒𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚. 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐥𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐥 𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐤.

This is why I would not build an AI compliance programme around a catalogue of laws alone.

I would interrogate every material AI use case across at least five dimensions:

𝐃𝐀𝐓𝐀 — What enters the system? Personal, biometric, health, financial, copyrighted, confidential?

𝐏𝐔𝐑𝐏𝐎𝐒𝐄 — Why is it being processed? Training, inference, profiling, recommendation or decision-making?

𝐈𝐌𝐏𝐀𝐂𝐓 — Does the output merely assist a human, or materially affect someone’s employment, credit, healthcare or rights?

𝐑𝐎𝐋𝐄 — Are we developing the model, deploying it, integrating a third-party model or merely procuring an AI service?

𝐉𝐔𝐑𝐈𝐒𝐃𝐈𝐂𝐓𝐈𝐎𝐍 — Where are the individuals, systems, providers and data located?

Only then should we ask:

𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐥𝐚𝐰𝐬 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐲?

And increasingly, there may be several simultaneously.

Privacy law may govern the personal data.

Copyright law may govern training material.

Employment law may become relevant to AI-assisted hiring.

Consumer law may govern representations or algorithmic practices.

Cybersecurity obligations may govern access and resilience.

Contract law may determine what the AI vendor can do with prompts, outputs and uploaded information.

And the EU AI Act may impose another layer depending upon the system, role and use case.

This leads to a practical governance architecture:
